title: MoTo: Mixture of Tokenizers Towards Fair Multilingual Language Modeling
claim: Modular per-language tokenizers merge into one shared vocabulary, and a language-ID router selects the tokenizer for each input.
layout: 2 panels, left vocabulary construction, right top-to-bottom pipeline, purple routing highlight
description: The figure has two panels separated by a vertical line. The left panel, titled Cross-Lingual Superset Vocabulary Construction, stacks three rounded boxes: English (purple), Chinese (red) and Turkish (teal). Each box shows how the words 'peace', 'barış' and '和平' are split into color-coded token chips. Native words are single tokens. Non-native words break into fragments or grey byte tokens such as 0xE5. Grey arrows run from the chips into a grey Superset V_S box on the right of the panel, where shared tokens are merged into one entry. The right panel, titled Mixture-of-Tokenizers Pipeline, is a vertical flow. An English input goes to Lang ID, which routes to English, Turkish, ... or Chinese. The selected path is a bold purple arrow and the inactive paths are faint. The flow continues through SS embedding, a dark Transformer (LLaMA 3.2) block and SS unembedding. It routes again and ends at next-token prediction.
caption: Left: Superset Vocabulary construction. Language-specific subword tokenizers are trained on their corresponding corpus. Words native to that language tend to be represented with fewer tokens, while non-native words fall back to coarser subwords or byte-level tokens. The superset vocabulary $\mathcal{V}_S$ is constructed by taking the union of all tokenizer vocabularies, assigning shared tokens a single global index, with $\lvert \mathcal{V}_S\rvert \leq \sum_i \lvert T_i\rvert$. Right: Mixture-of-Tokenizers (MoTo) pipeline. A tokenizer is selected based on the input language ID. The input is encoded into superset indices, processed by the transformer, and decoded back with the tokens from the superset, additionally it can utilize rules from the input tokenizer.
abstract: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.
